title: How Git Actually Stores Your History (Hint: Not Diffs)
subtitle: Most people think Git saves the changes between versions. It doesn't — it saves whole snapshots, and a single idea makes that cheap.
hook: Ask a room of developers how Git stores history and most will say "it saves the diffs between commits." It's a reasonable guess. It's also wrong. Git stores **complete snapshots** of your project at every commit — and it gets away with that because of one elegant trick: it names every piece of content by a hash of the content itself. Understand that, and Git stops feeling like magic incantations and starts making sense.

sections.heading: Content-addressed storage
sections.body:
At its core Git is a **key-value store** where the key is derived from the value. Take any file's contents, run it through a hash function (SHA-1, now moving to SHA-256), and you get a 40-character fingerprint like `d670460b...`. Git stores the file's contents under that fingerprint. This object is called a **blob**.

The consequence is quietly powerful: two identical files — or the same file across a hundred commits — hash to the *same* key, so Git stores the content **exactly once**. Nothing is duplicated. Change one byte and you get a completely different hash, hence a new object. That's why snapshots aren't wasteful.

sections.heading: Three object types, one structure
sections.body:
Everything in Git's database is one of three objects:

- **blob** — the contents of a file (no name, no metadata, just bytes).
- **tree** — a directory listing: filenames and permissions, each pointing to a blob or another tree.
- **commit** — a snapshot pointer: it names one top-level tree, the parent commit(s), the author, and the message.

String them together and a commit is just a node that points to a full tree of your project, which points to blobs. Each commit also points back to its parent — that backward chain *is* your history.

sections.caption: A commit points to a tree (your directory), the tree points to blobs (file contents), and each commit points to its parent. Everything is addressed by content hash.

sections.heading: What `git commit` really does
items: Hash the contents of each changed file and store it as a **blob** (unchanged files reuse their existing blob — same content, same hash).
Build **tree** objects capturing the directory structure and which blob each filename points to.
Create a **commit** object pointing to the top tree, your parent commit, and the message.
Move the current **branch pointer** forward to this new commit. That's it — history is now one link longer.

sections.label: Branches are almost nothing
sections.body: A branch in Git is just a **41-byte file** containing the hash of one commit. `HEAD` is a pointer to the branch you're on. Creating a branch doesn't copy anything — it writes one small pointer. This is why branching in Git is instant, and why it changed how teams work compared to older systems that physically duplicated files.

sections.caption: A hands-on tour of Git's object model — blobs, trees, commits, and the SHA that ties them together.

sections.label: Why rebasing 'rewrites history'
sections.body: Because a commit's hash is computed from its contents *including its parent and message*, changing anything about a commit produces a brand-new hash — a different object. Commands like `rebase` and `amend` don't edit commits in place; they create new ones and move the branch pointer to them. The old commits linger unreferenced until garbage collection. That's also why force-pushing a rebased branch can clobber collaborators: their history now points at objects yours abandoned.

takeaways: Git stores full **snapshots**, not diffs — and dedupes them by hashing content.
Everything is one of three objects: **blob** (file contents), **tree** (directory), **commit** (snapshot pointer).
Identical content hashes to the same key, so it's stored only once — snapshots stay cheap.
A **branch is just a pointer** (a hash in a tiny file); that's why branching is instant.
Rebase/amend create *new* commits with new hashes rather than editing in place — hence 'rewriting history'.
